title: Pupusas
subtitle: stuffed with savory jackfruit
menu_blurb: Griddled masa cakes filled with spiced jackfruit and onion. Crispy outside, soft inside, and best with salsa and a simple cabbage salad.
intro: A very flavorful Salvadoran treat! Crispy on the outside and soft on the inside, best served with salsa and a simple cabbage salad.
origin: The pupusa is the national dish of El Salvador, with origins reaching back some 2,000 to 3,000 years to the Indigenous Pipil people.

mise_en_place.label: Make
mise_en_place.task: The dough, then let it rest for 20 minutes

mise_en_place.label: Chop
mise_en_place.task: Onion and jackfruit, then cook the filling and let it cool

items.name: Masa harina (not corn flour or cornmeal)

steps.title: Make the dough
instructions: In a large bowl, mix the masa harina and salt. Add the spices if you like; in my opinion they add more flavor.
Pour the cold water over and stir with a spatula. When it gets hard to stir, knead by hand for 1 to 2 minutes until it feels like clay.
The dough will be slightly wet. Set it aside to rest for 15 to 20 minutes.

steps.title: Cook the filling
instructions: Finely chop the onion and jackfruit.
Cook in a little olive oil, add the spices, and cook until soft.
Remove from the heat and let it cool.

steps.title: Shape the pupusas
instructions: Wet your hands slightly and scoop out a ball of dough, about 3 tbsp.
Flatten it into a thick, even circle in the palm of your hand.
Fill the center with no more than 2 tsp of filling.
Close your hand to fold the dough into a pocket, and pinch the edges to seal.

steps.title: Griddle
instructions: Cook on a griddle or skillet over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes per side.
They are ready when golden and crispy with dark spots.

steps.title: Serve
instructions: Serve with salsa, cabbage salad, and/or guacamole.

tips.label: Flavor boost
tips.tip: Add more paprika, cumin, and salt as needed.

tips.label: Substitution
tips.tip: Fill with ⅓ cup of black or refried beans instead.

tips.label: Meal prep hack
tips.tip: Keeps in the fridge for several days, and freezes well.

nutrition.notes: Very low in sugar and cholesterol-free, and high in potassium and vitamin C.
Rich in antioxidants like quercetin and prebiotic fibers, supporting gut health and heart health by helping lower cholesterol and blood pressure.
Nixtamalization unlocks niacin (vitamin B3), calcium, iron, zinc and other B vitamins. Gluten-free with a low glycemic index.

notebook.question: What’s the difference between masa harina, corn flour, and cornmeal?
answer: They all come from corn, but only masa harina makes a dough that holds together.

table.label: Masa harina
table.text: Made from corn soaked and cooked in an alkaline solution (nixtamalization). This lets it bind with water into a pliable dough, and makes niacin easier to absorb.

table.label: Corn flour
table.text: Dried corn ground into a fine powder. It isn’t nixtamalized, so a tortilla made with it will crumble. (In the UK, “corn flour” means cornstarch.)

table.label: Cornmeal
table.text: A coarser grind of dried corn, used for crunch, like in cornbread. It doesn’t bind like masa harina.

notebook.question: Can they be substituted?
answer: Generally, no. Cornmeal and corn flour won’t form a cohesive dough for tortillas or pupusas without added binders like wheat flour. Masa harina can sometimes stand in for finely ground cornmeal in baking, adding a savory depth.

notebook.question: What is jackfruit?
answer: Jackfruit is a nutrient-dense tropical fruit, with India as its top producer. Some canned jackfruit is now marketed for its prebiotic fiber, which supports gut health.

notebook.question: What else can you use jackfruit for?
answer: It’s best known as a “pulled pork” substitute, but it has become far more versatile.

benefits.label: Seafood alternatives
benefits.text: Its flaky texture works for vegan “crab” cakes, “tuna” salad, or ceviche.
